newPageBriefs.contributionAndEvidence: Decision gap: readers treat annuity and 401(k) as alternatives; the sources show they sit at different layers. Evidence basis: reported (no numerical model; payout figures depend on insurer rates, age and contract, which no public source fixes). Sources: Investor.gov annuities page (captured verbatim 2026-11-16) and IRS retirement topics: contributions page ($24,500 for 2026, $23,500 for 2025; captured verbatim 2026-11-16). Reasoning trail in readiness.md. Attribution names the SEC Office of Investor Education and the IRS; no "our test" claims. Counterexample: a person with no employer plan has no 401(k) to compare, so the question becomes annuity vs IRA.

newPageBriefs.testingAndReview: Annuities and retirement plans are financial products/services: section G excludes them from testing claims. Decision: ordinary presentation; no testing language. Attribution is source-only (Investor.gov, IRS). Review profile HIGH (consequential retirement/investment claims) with 2-round ceiling and no named professional review required by the site content standard (YMYL categorization alone does not require one); IRS early-distribution, 401(k) basics and contributions pages captured verbatim 2026-11-16; disclaimer at bottom only; no guaranteed-return claims.
newPageBriefs.takeaway: If your employer plan offers a match, the IRS says matching contributions are allowed when the plan permits and may be discretionary, so check your plan: a match is available only through the 401(k), which makes it a conditional first step rather than a rule. An annuity answers a different question, guaranteed income, and Investor.gov says annuities suit long time horizons, carry surrender charges and fees, and warrants caution when bought inside a traditional 401(k) or IRA. The answer changes if you have no employer plan, if your plan has no match, or if you are near retirement and need income. Attributed to the IRS and Investor.gov, not to our testing; this is general education, not advice.

newPageBriefs.contributionAndEvidence: Decision gap: readers need the spending level at which the rotating 5% beats the higher flat rate. Evidence basis: calculated. In our internal cost modeling, we compared annual cash back on both cards across five spending patterns using Chase's published earn rates (flex_vs_unlimited.py, output flex_vs_unlimited.out.json). Inputs sourced from creditcards.chase.com Flex and Unlimited pages captured verbatim 2026-11-16. Assumptions: $24,000 annual spend, bonus-category spend fully matches the quarter's category, category activated, no sign-up bonus counted, $0 annual fees, bonus category excludes dining/drugstore/travel overlap. Break-even rule from the script: Flex beats Unlimited only if quarterly bonus-category spend B (capped at $1,500) satisfies 4B x 3.5% > other annual spend x 0.5%, i.e. annual bonus-category spend 4B is at least 12.5% of total annual spend S (B >= S x 0.03125 per quarter); maximum Flex advantage is $210 a year minus 0.5% of all other spend, so Flex cannot win at roughly $48,000 or more total annual spend. Counterexample: a Flex holder who does not activate the bonus earns $120 less than Unlimited on $24,000 of spend.
newPageBriefs.tablesToolsVisuals: Static comparison table plus a finite break-even table by quarterly bonus-category spend (0 to $1,500); no interactive widget because the single break-even number and finite scenarios answer the decision.
newPageBriefs.testingAndReview: Credit cards are financial products: section G excludes them from testing claims. Decision: ordinary presentation; no "we tested". newPageBriefs.takeaway: Choose Freedom Unlimited if your spend is spread across ordinary purchases, your total annual spend is about $48,000 or more, or you will not track quarterly categories. The answer changes if Chase changes rates, quarterly categories or the 15-month 0% APR; check chase.com for current terms.
